brief_data.deck: Walden Robotics, the Toyota Research Institute spin-out whose wheeled, two-armed robots have worked a Toyota plant floor since February, came out of stealth on 15 July with a $300M seed at a $1.1B valuation, co-led by Toyota and Deviation Capital, with Nvidia, Boeing and Samsung Ventures behind it.

risks.label: A SEED-STAGE MARKETING BUDGET
risks.detail: The $300M funds robots and deployments; no chief marketing officer or marketing function owns a sponsorship.
risks.counter: Enter at partner tier, part-paid in deployments; sell it as a reference customer and a recruiting stage.

risks.label: TOYOTA'S PORTFOLIO, NOT ITS BRAND
risks.detail: Toyota is an investor, not the owner; a Walden logo on a TGR-titled car needs TGR's comfort.
risks.counter: Open through the investor; Williams is the fallback if TGR declines.

gridfit.detail: no rival in this category lane

gridfit.label: OPEN
gridfit.detail: no rival in this category lane

extended.ask: A 25-minute call with Russ Tedrake before the United States GP, opened alongside the Toyota investor relationship, to test appetite for a 2027 start, agree a winter-build pilot at Kannapolis as year one, and size an Official Robotics Partner entry at TGR Haas F1 Team, part-paid in deployments, with a US announcement.

value.text: Walden robots deployed on the Kannapolis and Banbury floors: tending the team's CNC machines, tool setting, kitting parts for the car build and loading and unloading between stations, the same tasks they run in shifts alongside human teams at Toyota. The pilot-to-production cycle at Toyota was under two months, which fits inside a winter build. The team gets capacity in a workforce-constrained shop; Walden gets its first non-automotive-OEM reference deployment in a factory the whole industry watches.
value.label: Operational workstream (Mode A)

value.text: A $1.1B partner entering at partner tier in the first year of the Toyota era, with Nvidia, Boeing, Samsung and CoreWeave on its cap table and manufacturers as its customers: Austin and Las Vegas hospitality that brings the automotive, aerospace and semiconductor buyers the team's other technology partners want to meet.
value.label: Commercial lift for the team

value.text: A factory-floor content series on robots building a race car, co-produced with the team's operations group, plus the recruiting stage a company hiring against a $300M seed needs: MIT and Toyota Research Institute engineers watching their robots on a Formula 1 floor.
value.label: Content and ecosystem

value.text: Official Robotics Partner designation, sidepod and garage placement, naming of the Kannapolis robot cell, Austin and Las Vegas hospitality, and driver and engineering access for Walden's channels.
value.label: What the team gives back

why_now.text: On 15 July 2026 Walden Robotics came out of stealth with a $300M seed at a $1.1B valuation, co-led by Toyota (Toyota Motor Corporation, Toyota Invention Partners and Toyota Ventures) and Deviation Capital, with Nvidia, Boeing, AE Ventures, Samsung Ventures, Prologis Ventures and CoreWeave Ventures as strategic investors and Menlo Ventures, NextView, Squarepoint Capital and others alongside. The Boston Globe called it one of the Boston area's biggest robotics deals ever.
why_now.label: Trigger

why_now.text: The company spun out of Toyota Research Institute in January 2026 and had robots doing production work at a Toyota plant in North America by February, moving from first pilot to real work in under two months. Its own line is that the hard problem in robotics is now deployment, not research. A company selling deployments to manufacturers needs a stage where manufacturers, engineers and recruits are watching, and a Formula 1 factory is one.
why_now.label: A deployment company, not a lab

why_now.text: The seed is 64 days old on the issue date, inside the desk's 90-day window but not fresh, which is why timing scores 14 and not 18. What keeps it live is the calendar: 2027 partner rosters close in the fourth quarter, and the winter build from December to February is exactly when a factory-floor pilot can run without touching a race weekend.
why_now.label: Two months old, still inside the window

why_now.text: The United States GP in Austin in late October and the Las Vegas GP in November are the two US rounds left in 2026. A deal agreed before Austin can be announced in the United States and put robots on the Kannapolis floor for the 2027 car build.
why_now.label: Calendar window

why_team.text: Toyota Gazoo Racing replaced MoneyGram as Haas's title partner from 2026, on top of the technical partnership signed in October 2024 that covers vehicle development, wind-tunnel testing, carbon-fibre parts and a simulator at Banbury, under the banner People, Product, Pipeline. Toyota co-led Walden's seed through Toyota Motor Corporation, Toyota Invention Partners and Toyota Ventures, and Tedrake spent a decade inside Toyota Research Institute. No other team on the grid has a path this short.
why_team.label: The introduction runs through the investor

why_team.text: Haas is owned by Gene Haas, founder of Haas Automation, the largest CNC machine-tool builder in North America, and the team's CNC shop is central to operations at Kannapolis. Machine tending, tool setting and parts kitting are the tasks Walden's robots already do in shifts at Toyota. The workstream is not a metaphor: the robots would tend the machines the owner's company builds.
why_team.label: A team that already builds with machines

why_team.text: No robotics brand sits on any F1 roster in 2026. Formula E is closed: ABB, a global robotics and automation group, has been the championship's title partner since 2018, so a rival robotics brand has no home there, which is why the 10 September pool pointer at Jaguar TCS Racing is wrong. In F1, Siemens holds the industrial-automation lane at Oracle Red Bull Racing and Visa Cash App Racing Bulls, and every carmaker-aligned team is awkward for a Toyota-backed company. Haas and Williams are the independents, and only Haas carries the Toyota name.
why_team.label: The only lane on either grid

why_team.text: Austin in late October and Las Vegas in November, with the Kannapolis factory an hour from Charlotte for a US press moment, and the Banbury base for the European season.
why_team.label: Where it activates

ruled_out.reason: ABB, a robotics and automation group, is the championship's title partner since 2018; a rival robotics brand has no lane in the series. The 10 September pool pointer at Jaguar TCS Racing is withdrawn.

brief_data.bottom_line: $300M at $1.1B on 15 July, robots at work in a Toyota plant since February, the Toyota-titled team with its own CNC shop, and no robotics brand on the grid. No marketing chief and a two-month-old trigger hold it at 70.

brief_data.the_case_p1: The company was founded in January 2026 out of Toyota Research Institute by Russ Tedrake, the MIT professor who ran TRI's large-behavior-model work. Its robots have two arms and a sensor head on a wheeled base, no legs, and run on Large Behavior Models that learn a task through practice. At a Toyota plant in North America they went from first pilot to production in under two months and now run shifts alongside human teams: machine tending, tool setting, parts kitting, loading and unloading. Strategic partners span automotive, aerospace, semiconductors, electronics and logistics.
brief_data.the_case_p2: No robotics brand sits on the 2026 F1 grid, and the one team titled by Walden's lead investor runs its own CNC shop: Haas is owned by Gene Haas, founder of Haas Automation, the largest CNC machine-tool builder in North America. Machine tending is the task Walden's robots already do at Toyota. The lane is open and the workstream is literal.

brief_data.why_team_para: Toyota Gazoo Racing took the title at Haas from 2026 after a 2024 technical partnership, and Toyota co-led Walden's seed: the introduction runs through the investor. Haas is the American privateer, based in Kannapolis and Banbury, with a CNC shop at the centre of its operations. Formula E is closed to the category: ABB, a robotics and automation group, has been its title partner since 2018. Carmaker-aligned teams are awkward for a Toyota-backed company; Williams is the only other independent.
brief_data.deal_arch_para: Entry as Official Robotics Partner. <font name='Poppins-Bold' size='9.5'>THREE YEARS</font>, 2027-2029, spanning the first deployments beyond Toyota and two car builds. Estimated $3-5M a year, part-payable in robot deployments the team would otherwise staff. Scope: sidepod placement, naming of the Kannapolis robot cell, Austin and Las Vegas hospitality, and a factory content series.
brief_data.why_now_callout: <font name='Poppins-Bold' size='9'>WHY NOW</font>  The seed closed on 15 July and the deployments it funds are the story; a company hiring against a $300M cheque needs a stage engineers watch. Teams close 2027 rosters in the fourth quarter, Austin and Las Vegas sit inside the window, and the winter build is when a factory pilot runs.
brief_data.decision_maker_bio: Tedrake is an MIT professor who spent a decade at Toyota Research Institute, latterly senior vice president of large behavior models. No chief marketing officer is listed. Path: Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer; Ben Burchfiel, co-founder and Chief Technology Officer; Dave Johnson, Chief Product Officer.
brief_data.decision_maker_role: Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer, Walden Robotics
brief_data.opening_angle_intro: Lead with the CNC shop, not the logo.
brief_data.opening_angle_quote: “Russ, your lead investor's racing arm puts its name on the one F1 team that runs its own CNC shop, your robots already tend Toyota's machines, and nobody on the grid has a robotics partner. 25 minutes before Austin?”
